text: Across 307 purchase months from January 1991 to July 2016, a buyer who held a home for 10 years ended ahead of an identical renter in 75.6% of them (median $157,104 ahead on a $400,000 home), with no investing of the difference.
The worst start was June 2006: the home index rose only 3.2% in 10 years and the buyer ended $82,385 behind the renter.
The best start was April 2012, at a 3.91% mortgage rate: the index rose 114.3% and the buyer ended $483,975 ahead.
By start period: 1990s buyers were ahead in 100.0% of 10-year windows, 2002-2007 buyers in 8.3%, and 2009-2016 buyers in 100.0%.
Holding period matters: the buyer was ahead in 74.4% of 5-year windows and 100.0% of 15-year windows (worst 15-year start November 2005, still $79,829 ahead).

The result leans on the starting rent: with today's rent set at 5.0% of the price a year the 10-year share is 75.6%; at 4% it is 64.2%, at 6% it is 92.2%; if the renter's savings earn 3-month T-bill rates it is 66.4%.
Most people expect buying to win almost always, because rent is 'thrown away'; in this replay the renter still came out ahead in 75 of 307 10-year windows.
note: Guess about beliefs (market dossier: 'thrown away' is the misconception competitors rebut); the check is only that the renter won some but not all windows. Not evidence of what viewers believe.

text: Every 10-year start where the renter came out ahead fell between April 2001 and December 2007, when starting rent was low next to the price (at most 6.43% a year, against a median of 6.71%).
note: Same 10-year set for every number; the check also requires the largest renter-win yield to be below the median yield.

text: At the September 2026 average rate of 6.86%, the buyer's first month costs $2,933 against $1,667 rent, so rent is 56.8% of the buyer's outlay: lower than at any of the 307 replayed start months (lowest 57.9%, July 2006).
note: Today's month-1 figures use the anchor rent yield and the latest complete rate month; the ranking is independent of the 5% anchor because rent scales the same way at every start.

text: The home is the national FHFA index, not one house: in the worst window the national index rose 3.2%; a single home or city can do much better or worse.
note: Number from the worst window; the second clause is a caveat, not a measured claim.

text: History, not a forecast: the last window used ends in July 2026, the last month of the price index.
note: Check: last_10y + 120 months = hpi_last; nothing extrapolated.
